newsitem.title: USA: Dole plans to get tough in final presidential debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole plans to get tough in final presidential debate.

text.p: Republican challenger Bob Dole goes into Wednesday's final debate with President Bill Clinton planning to get tough on ethical issues.
Lowering expectations before the clash that Dole must win to pull up to Clinton in polls, his press secretary, Nelson Warfield, said Clinton "goes into this a prohibitive favourite."
Dole "prepped for the debate" at his hotel with aides on Tuesday before a luncheon speech to a business group, a staffer said.

With three weeks to the election on Nov. 5, Dole is running far behind in most polls nationally with the latest CNN/USA Today/Gallup tracking poll putting him 18 points behind Clinton, 54 to 36 percent, with Ross Perot at 4 percent.
After the first debate, people told pollsters they believed Dole scored points on congeniality but that Clinton won the contest.

Like the first debate, Wednesday's contest at the University of San Diego will also be 90 minutes long. It will have a town meeting format with citizens quizzing the candidates unlike the Hartford bout where questions were asked by a single moderator, public television anchor Jim Lehrer.

Since the first debate, Dole has been urged by some aides to toughen his questioning of Clinton on character matters. Others have argued a get-tough attitude is risky for Dole who wants to avoid reminders of earlier characterisations of him as mean spirited, especially as former President Gerald Ford's 1976 running mate.
Dole signalled on Monday that he will go on the attack in the final debate although his press secretary said that Dole "is not going to make any personal attacks."

Instead, he will focus on what the campaign sees as legitimate issues, such as collection of personal and confidential FBI files of Republicans by White House aides and Clinton's alleged links to an Indonesian banking combine.

At a Kansas City rally on Monday, Dole called the Clinton White House unethical and compared the FBI files matter -- now being called "Filegate" -- with the Watergate scandal of the Richard Nixon administration.
"There were people who went to jail in the Nixon administration for looking at two FBI files. They've (the White House) got 900 files," Dole told the rally.

Dole said: "Over 30 people -- about 30 people are already gone. They're in jail or they're indicted or they're out of there. Then he talks about an ethical administration. He does not have an ethical administration. "
"And we're going to go after him on that in the debate on Wednesday night."

Dole also later demanded that Clinton explain $425,000 in contributions to the Democratic Party from a couple with links to the Lippo Group banking conglomerate in Indonesia, controlled by the Riady family who had banking interests in Clinton's Arkansas and has visited the White House.

Republicans, such as House Speaker Newt Gingrich, have attacked the contributions as possibly illegal and Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain has called for a special prosecutor to investigate the foreign contributions.
"We're going to raise the questions every day until the president's properly responded," Dole said. "Not some slip, slide and duck, Mr. President. Just answer the questions,"
In Albuquerque, New Mexico, where Clinton was preparing for the debate, Clinton's campaign press secretary Joe Lockhart dismissed Dole's attacks on the contributions as a "moment of desperation."
